outcomes.name: query_plan
outcomes.answer:
The planner chose a **sequential scan** (`Seq Scan`) for this query.

Here is the plan from `EXPLAIN` (I didn't use `ANALYZE`, so the query wasn't actually run):

```
Seq Scan on users  (cost=0.00..1.04 rows=1 width=56)
  Filter: (id = 1)
```

It reads the whole `users` table and keeps only rows where `id = 1`. The estimated total cost is 1.04, which suggests the table is very small, probably a single page. I didn't check whether `id` has an index. Even if it does, PostgreSQL normally picks a sequential scan on a table this small because it's cheaper than using the index.

outcomes.name: unused_index
outcomes.answer:
statistics started being collected. A crash or restore can also wipe the counts, so check how long this database has been running before acting on the list.

Seven of the nine are primary keys or unique constraints. They enforce data rules even when no query reads them, so they aren't candidates for removal. **`idx_users_bio`** is the only ordinary index on the list, so it's the only one that looks safe to drop. `order_summary_user_id_idx` is also unique, and `order_summary` may be a materialized view. If it is, a unique index is required for `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY`, so leave it in place.

**Answer:** `api_keys_pkey`, `customers_pkey`, `order_items_pkey`, `order_summary_user_id_idx`, `payments_pkey`, `tickets_pkey`, `idx_users_bio`, `users_username_key`, `warehouses_pkey`

outcomes.name: largest_table
outcomes.answer:
**`public.users`** uses the most disk: **64 kB (65,536 bytes)** in total. That includes 8 kB of table data and 48 kB of indexes, with TOAST and other storage making up the rest.

I got this from `pg_total_relation_size` across all tables and materialized views in `public`. The next largest tables are `customers`, `warehouses`, `shipping_regions` and `tickets`, at 32 kB each. Every table here is very small, so the gap between them is only a few pages. If a table were split into partitions, each partition would be counted on its own rather than added together under the parent.

outcomes.name: function_source
outcomes.answer:
sn't set a "modified" column. This is the line that does it:

```sql
BEGIN NEW.created_at = now(); RETURN NEW; END;
```

The only trigger that uses it is `trg_orders_modified` on `public.orders`, which runs `BEFORE UPDATE ... FOR EACH ROW`.

**What this means:** every time a row in `orders` is updated, its `created_at` is reset to the time of the update, so the original creation time is lost. The `orders` table has only `id`, `user_id`, `status` and `created_at`, with no `updated_at` or `modified_at` column. My guess is that the function was meant to track modification time but writes to the wrong column. That would be a bug, and nothing in the schema confirms what was intended.

**Answer:** on every update to an `orders` row, it sets `created_at` to `now()`, via `NEW.created_at = now();`.

outcomes.name: triggers_on_orders
outcomes.answer:
The `public.orders` table has one trigger, and it calls `update_modified_column()`.

| Trigger | When it fires | Function | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| `trg_orders_modified` | `BEFORE UPDATE`, once for each row | `update_modified_column()` | enabled |

Definition:
```sql
CREATE TRIGGER trg_orders_modified BEFORE UPDATE ON public.orders
FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION update_modified_column()
```

I didn't look at the function's code. Its name suggests it sets a "last modified" timestamp when a row is updated, but that's a guess.

outcomes.name: rls_policies
outcomes.answer:

  - **WITH CHECK:** none.
  - **Roles:** the tool returned an empty roles list. I take that to mean the policy applies to all roles (PUBLIC), but that's my reading, not something the tool stated.

Things to watch for:
- **Forced RLS is off.** The table owner, superusers and roles with `BYPASSRLS` skip the policy and see every row.
- **No other commands are covered.** There are no `INSERT`, `UPDATE` or `DELETE` policies. With RLS on, a role that isn't exempt can't do those operations on any row, even if it has the table privileges.
- **Unset setting hides everything.** If `app.current_user_id` isn't set, `current_setting(..., true)` returns NULL and that session sees no orders.

outcomes.name: view_definition
outcomes.answer:
I pulled the `active_orders` view definition from the database (it has no description set):

```sql
SELECT o.id,
       o.user_id,
       u.username,
       o.status,
       o.created_at
FROM orders o
JOIN users u ON o.user_id = u.id
WHERE o.status <> 'delivered'::order_status;
```

**It excludes only the `delivered` status.** Every other `order_status` value stays in the view, which probably includes cancelled orders. I haven't checked which values that enum contains.

Because it uses an inner join to `users`, the view also leaves out any order whose `user_id` doesn't match a user. That includes orders where `user_id` is NULL.

outcomes.name: sequence_exhaustion
outcomes.answer:
countdown` is the sequence closest to running out.** It has about 1,000 values left. All the other sequences have about 2.1 billion left.

The health check lists every sequence as 0.00% consumed, but that figure is wrong for `countdown`. It counts down instead of up, and the check only works for sequences that count up.

| Sequence | Last value | Step | Limit | Values left |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **countdown** | 1000 (already used) | −1 | 0 | **1,000** (999 down to 0) |
| tickets_id_seq | 5 | +1 | 2,147,483,647 | ~2.1 billion |
| users/products/orders_id_seq | 3 | +1 | 2,147,483,647 | ~2.1 billion |
| others | 1–2 | +1 | 2,147,483,647 | ~2.1 billion |

`countdown` doesn't wrap around when it hits its limit. After about 1,000 more calls to `nextval`, the next call will fail with an error.

outcomes.name: matview_concurrent_refresh
outcomes.answer:
id_idx` is defined as `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX order_summary_user_id_idx ON public.order_summary USING btree (user_id)`. PostgreSQL requires a unique index on plain columns, not expressions, with no `WHERE` clause. This index is valid, unique, built on a plain column and not partial.
2. **It is already populated** (`ispopulated = true`). A concurrent refresh doesn't work on a view that has never been populated.

The index also fits the view's data. The view groups by `u.id, u.username` and selects `u.id AS user_id`, so there is one row per user and `user_id` is unique.

A concurrent refresh lets reads continue during the refresh. It is usually slower than a normal refresh because it compares the old and new results to work out which rows changed. Only one refresh of the view can run at a time.
